text:
Hypothalamus : Ventral topographic division of the vertebrate interbrain; the thalamus is the dorsal topographic division.

Interbrain :  A  topographic  division  that  includes  the  thalamus  and hypothalamus, which form the rostral end of the vertebrate brainstem (and the caudal part of the forebrain), between the cerebral hemisphere (endbrain) and midbrain; it contains the third ventricle. A synonym is diencephalon.

Interneuron : In the original sense, any neuron intercalated between a sensory neuron and a motor neuron; intraregional interneurons have an axon that ramifi  es entirely within its parent gray matter region, whereas interregional interneurons have an axon trunk that extends outside the parent gray matter region to more or less distant regions, although the trunk often issues intraregional axon collaterals as well.

Isocortex :  A vast expanse of mammalian cerebral cortex that can be divided  into  six  layers,  or  at  least  supposedly  passes  through  a  sixlayered  stage  during  embryogenesis;  neocortex  is  a  nonpreferred synonym because it is based on outdated evolutionary theories.

Lateral : Away from the median plane in the frontal plane; as opposed to medial.

Local circuit (inter)neuron  : See Interneuron (intraregional).

Longitudinal axis : The oral-aboral axis of the body in all animals with a nervous system; it is perpendicular to the transverse axis. Synonyms include rostrocaudal axis, central axis, long axis, midsagittal axis, principal axis, and anteroposterior axis, the last being discouraged as especially ambiguous in comparative anatomy. It is a conceptual axis because it is usually curved to a greater or lesser extent at different stages of development, in the adults of different species, and even in particular adult individuals during the course of a day.

Medial : Toward the median plane in the frontal plane, as opposed to lateral.

Median plane : The sagittal plane dividing the body into roughly equal right and left halves; synonyms include midline and midsagittal plane.

Mediolateral axis : In animals with bilateral symmetry an axis perpendicular to the rostrocaudal (longitudinal) axis that lies in the frontal plane. It is unusual in having a right and left half reflected across the median plane; that is, for the right and left sides of the body, medial is toward the median plane and lateral is toward the right or left edge of the body. A synonym is right-left axis.

Medulla :  Topographic  division  of  the  vertebrate  central  nervous system (cerebrospinal axis) between the pons rostrally and the spinal cord caudally. Current synonyms include medulla oblongata, bulb, and myelencephalon.

Metamere : See Segment.

Midbrain :  Topographic division of the vertebrate brain between the interbrain rostrally and the pons caudally and containing the cerebral aqueduct; a synonym is mesencephalon.

Neocortex  : Nonpreferred synonym for isocortex.

Nerve fiber  : An unmyelinated axon or a myelinated axon; literally accurate for the peripheral nervous system, but often applied (ambiguously) to the central nervous system as well.

Nerve net :  A  topographic  division  that  is  a  longitudinally  arranged nervous  system  with  radial  symmetry  and  relatively  evenly  and  diffusely  distributed  neurons,  characteristic  of  Coelenterates,  Ctenophores, Hemichordates,  Pogonophores,  and  adult  Echinoderms.  While  small neuron  condensations  (called  marginal  ganglia)  and  circular  zones (called nerve rings) with a higher concentration of neurons and neuron extensions can be present, nerves are not clearly diff  erentiated,  and nothing like a central nervous system is present; it is thus a nervous system  with  no  clear  topographic  divisions  -  a  divisionless  nervous system. The nervous system of hydra (a Coelenterate) is an example of a relatively simple diff  use nerve net, whereas the terminal plexuses in the wall of the mammalian digestive system can be viewed as analogous to a relatively diff  erentiated nerve net.

Neural network : The structural arrangement of all neurons and their connections in a nervous system. A neural network has a set of nodes (gray matter regions, neuron types, or individual neurons) and the connections (macro-, meso-, or microconnections, respectively) between them and other parts of the body like muscles and glands. A complete neural network can be distinguished from a neural subnetwork, which is  an  arbitrary  subset  of  the  complete  neural  network,  often  distinguished on functional grounds.

Neuraxis  : Central nervous system or cerebrospinal axis.

Neurite  : Term often used now for a neuron cytoplasmic extension when its identity as axon, dendrite, or amacrine extension is unclear.

Neuron: The basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system at the level of cells; the connections of neurons, which are established by way of chemical or electrical synapses, form the wiring diagram of the nervous system.

Neuron extension :  A  thin cytoplasmic projection from the cell body that  may  be  axon,  dendrite,  or  amacrine  extension;  nonpreferred synonyms inlude neuron process and neuron prolongation.

Neuron population : An arbitrarily defined set of neurons that may or may not correspond exactly to a specific gray matter region or neuron type. For example, a neuron population is formed by a subset of the individual neurons that together constitute a neuron type. In contrast, however, all neurons within an anterograde pathway tracer injection site that spreads to involve multiple adjacent gray matter regions, or an irregular extent within a single gray matter region, form the neuron population associated with that injection site. Another example of this type  would  be  all  neurons  within  multiple  gray  matter  regions  that project to a single gray matter region  -  as demonstrated, for example, by a retrograde pathway tracer injection site. A third example would be all neurons in a topographic division like the hypothalamus that express the  corticotropin-releasing  hormone  (CRH)  gene  following  hypovolemic stress, as demonstrated by in situ hybridization. In general, a site contains a neuron population.

Neuron process  : See Neuron extension.

Neuron  type :  For  purposes  of  wiring  diagrams,  neuron  types  are defined and classifi  ed primarily by their connections and, secondarily by their location, shape, size, and gene expression profi  le. Neurons can be placed in a seven-level taxonomic hierarchy, with neuron types occupying  a  level  equivalent  to  species  in  animal  taxonomy.  Formally,  a neuron type is  defined  as  a  distinct  cluster  in  polythetic  parametric space, with the main parameter being connections, secondary parameters being location, shape, size, and gene expression profi  le, and tertiary parameters also helpful. An example of a neuron type is blue cone, of  the  neuron  group cone, of the neuron class photoreceptor, of the neuron category visual, of the neuron division sensory, of the cell type neuron, with no known neuron varieties of this neuron type, at least in  rat.  Neuron  types  can  consist  of  a  single  identified  neuron  (most common for invertebrates) or a set of neurons sharing the same parametric space.

Neuropil :  The gray matter compartment exclusive of cell bodies and vascular cells, thus consisting of the cytoplasmic extensions of neurons and glia, including synapses.

Neurotransmitter : A chemical messenger that is released from a presynaptic axon terminal and then diff  uses through the extracellular fl  uid to produce a response in a postsynaptic cell(s), usually by interacting with a specific receptor.

Node : The site of origin or of termination of a connection at the level of a  gray  matter region (macronode), neuron type (mesonode), or individual neuron (micronode).

Nucleus :  1)  A  typically  nonlaminated  diff  erentiation  of  gray  matter (a gray matter region) in the vertebrate central nervous system (term introduced in 1779 by Christian Ludwig); 2) the large organelle in the cell  body  that  contains  the  chromosomes  (term  introduced  1833  by Robert Brown).

Pallium : Synonym for cerebral cortex.

Pathway :  The  component  of  a  connection  that  is  demonstrated  in a specific tracing experiment or analysis.

Perikaryon : The cell body without the cell nucleus.

Peripheral  nervous  system :  In  animals  with  bilateral  symmetry, a topographic division that is an obvious condensation of the nervous system as a whole, generally extending transversely from the central nervous system and consisting of nerves and ganglia.

Plexus : A general term for a group of interconnecting neurons or nerve components that may be a sheet of interwoven fibers or a course mesh of communicating nerves, without or with neuron cell bodies, including  ganglia.  Examples include nerve nets, prevertebral plexuses, and spinal nerve plexuses (with postplexus spinal nerves distal to them).

Pons :  A  topographic  division  of  the  vertebrate  brain  between  the medulla caudally and the midbrain rostrally; the cerebellum is attached to it dorsally.

Process : See Neuron extension.

Projection : Synonym for connection.

Proxima l : Toward the origin of an object like a tentacle, limb, or nerve; as opposed to distal.

Region  :  Shortened  form  of  gray  matter  region,  though  other  definitions are found in the literature.

Rhombencephalon : Synonym for rhombicbrain.

Rhombicbrain : Topographic division of the vertebrate brain consisting of hindbrain (pons and cerebellum) and afterbrain (medulla); it lies between  the  spinal  cord  caudally  and  the  midbrain  rostrally  and contains the fourth ventricle. A synonym is rhombencephalon.

Rostral : Toward the mouth along the longitudinal (rostrocaudal) axis of the body, as opposed to caudal. Originally, toward the beak of a ship's prow ( rostrum ).

Rostrocaudal axis :  Equally acceptable synonym for longitudinal axis but also indicating polarity or direction toward the oral (rostral) end, or toward the aboral (caudal) end, of the axis.

Route : The physical course taken by a connection through gray matter regions and/or white matter tracts.

Sagittal plane : In animals with bilateral symmetry, the plane of section parallel to the longitudinal axis of the body and passing dorsoventral, parallel to the median plane, dividing the body into right and left parts. It is perpendicular to the other longitudinal plane, the frontal plane.

Segment : In topographic or regional anatomy, a modular unit that is repeated  serially  down  the  longitudinal  axis  of  the  body  during  early embryogenesis; toward the later stages of development these homologous units, which are also called metameres, may undergo secondary modifications so that in the adult all segments are not generally identical.

Site :  An arbitrarily defined point, area, or volume in the nervous system that may or may not correspond to a standard structural feature (term); examples include injection site,  labeling  site,  lesion  site,  stimulation site,  activation  site,  and  sampling  site.  A  site  encompasses  a  neuron population.

Soma : The cell body of a neuron, including the nucleus and surrounding cytoplasm, which is bounded by the plasma (outer) membrane; plural: somata.

Spinal cord : One of two major topographic divisions of the vertebrate central  nervous  system;  it  lies  caudal  the  other  major  division,  the brain, and contains the central canal part of the ventricles.

Sulcus : A groove or furrow on the surface of the brain; a deep sulcus is usually referred to as a fi  ssure.

Synapse :  Generally,  a  natural  junction  achieving  functional  conduction between distinct neurons, or a neuron and another cell, and accomplished through contact or near contact without regard to mechanism.

They are usually divided into chemical, electrical, and mixed synapses. The  most  common  in  adult  vertebrates,  the  chemical  synapse,  is  a structure-function diff  erentiation consisting of three parts: a neuronal presynaptic compartment where neurotransmitter is released from the terminal, a synaptic cleft of variable width, and a postsynaptic compartment that may or may not be neuronal but does have plasma membrane  receptors  for  neurotransmitters.  At  classical  unidirectional chemical synapses neurotransmitters may have feed-forward effects on the postsynaptic membranes and feedback effects on presynaptic membranes. It is thought, however, that these synapses are rectifi  ers, with neural network information fl  owing from presynaptic neuron to postsynaptic cell, modulated by presynaptic neurotransmitter feedback. In contrast,  reciprocal  or  bidirectional  chemical  synapses  release  neurotransmitter on both sides of the synaptic cleft and can thus transmit neural network information in either direction depending on network activity. Bidirectional chemical synapses are characteristic of amacrine extensions rather than axons. The distance between presynaptic membrane and postsynaptic membrane can vary enormously, from about 20-30 nm at classical chemical synapses like the neuromuscular junction, to microns for the sympathetic innervation of blood vessels, to centimeters  or  meters  for  neurotransmitter  released  into  the  blood. Electrical synapses are based strictly on the fl  ow of ions, rather than neurotransmitters. Finally, mixed synapses have the combined features of chemical and electrical synapses.

Synapse-of-passage : Synonym for terminal-of-passage.

Tectum :  The dorsal topographic division of the vertebrate midbrain; the ventral division is the tegmentum.

Tegmentum :  The  ventral  topographic  division  of  the  vertebrate midbrain; the dorsal division is the tectum.

Telencephalon: Synonym for endbrain (cerebrum, cerebral hemisphere).

Teleology: Explains  the  past  and  present  in  terms  of  the  future,  in contrast to mechanism, which explains the present and future in terms of the past; teleology is associated historically with vitalism in biology; it is the theory of purposes, ends, goals, fi  nal causes, and values  -  the Good (Russell, 1916).

Terminal bouton  : Synonym for axon terminal; bouton means 'button' in French.

Terminal : A general term that refers to an axon terminal and/or terminalof-passage; its characteristic feature is a slight rounded swelling that is presynaptic.

Terminal-of-passage :  An  axon  terminal  on  a  very  short  stalk  that protrudes from an axon trunk or axon collateral along its course rather than at the terminal arborization of the trunk or collateral. With the light microscope it resembles a dendritic spine.

Th alamus : The dorsal topographic division of the vertebrate interbrain; the ventral division is the hypothalamus.

Topographic description of body : One of two common orthogonal ways  of  describing  completely  the  body;  the  other  is  the  systems description of body. Topography here deals with the accurate geometric delineation and description of locations in the body. For mammals the major locations are head, neck, trunk, and extremities. A hierarchical set  of  topographic  locations  together  describes  completely  the  body from a structural perspective.

Transverse axis :  The axis perpendicular to the longitudinal (rostrocaudal) axis of the body in all animals with a nervous system.

Transverse plane :  A plane of section perpendicular to the longitudinal axis, dividing the body into rostral and caudal parts.

Varicosity : See Axon varicosity.

Ventral :  Toward the belly of the body, or away from the back, in the transverse plane; the opposite of dorsal.

White matter : A gross anatomical term referring to parts of the nervous system that are dominated by axons; in fresh tissue they appear white to the naked eye because many axons are surrounded by a whitish  myelin  sheath  that  is  mostly  lipid  (compare  with  gray  matter). However,  white  matter  is  often  a  mixture  of  myelinated  axons  and unmyelinated axons, and entire aggregates of axons can be unmyelinated. Th erefore, white matter is a generic term for a nervous system volume where axons are the predominant neural component, although of course glia and parts of the circulatory system, vascular cells, are also present.  White  matter  can  contain  scattered  neurons  that  may  be assigned  either  to  an  adjacent  gray  matter  region,  or  to  a  new  gray matter region embedded (nested) within the white matter; assignment depends on diff  erentiable neuron types involved. There is often a fuzzy border of variable width and difficult to measure between gray matter and white matter.

White matter tract :  A  recognizable division of white matter in the nervous system that can be bordered by gray matter, another white matter  tract(s),  or  nonneural  tissue.  Borders  between  white  matter tracts  are  determined  by  defined  structural  landmarks  and  are  commonly arbitrary.

Wiring diagram : An illustration of the physical arrangement of connections between a set of nodes  -  gray matter regions, neuron types, or neurons  -  in  the  nervous  system.  Wiring  diagrams  can  be  at  various levels of abstraction from three-dimensional models to two-dimensional schema, but a complete wiring diagram, by definition, includes route information. Compare with connectome.
